keep: Her own investor said she was wrong about the carpet. At ninety-six she opened next door anyway.
lede: She learned English from the words her daughter brought home from school and opened a furniture store with $500. The dealers she undersold took her to court, and the judge left with $1,400 of carpet.
copy: She left Russia at twenty-three by talking her way past a border guard, with no formal schooling and no English. In Omaha she learned the language in the evenings from her older daughter, who brought home each day's words from school. In 1937, after years of selling used clothing, she opened the Nebraska Furniture Mart with $500. The method was price. Omaha's retailers pressured the furniture and carpet makers not to sell to her; she found the stock by other routes and cut prices anyway. When the money ran out early on, she sold the furniture and appliances from her own home to pay her creditors on time. The dealers took her to court under the Fair Trade laws. She won every case. At the end of one, having shown the court she could sell carpet at a profit far below the going price, she sold the judge $1,400 of it.

In 1983 Warren Buffett bought control. His own letters do not agree on how much. The 1983 letter says Berkshire bought 90 per cent and optioned 10 per cent to young family managers; the 1992 letter says the family sold 80. Neither gives a price. The deal was done, he wrote ten years later, without audited financial statements, a check of the real estate records or any warranties. By then the Mart sold over $100 million a year out of one 200,000-square-foot store, and no other home furnishings store in the country came close. She was eighty-nine. She stayed on as chairman and sold carpet on the floor seven days a week.

It is easy to tell the next part as a founder pushed out at ninety-five. Buffett's letter for 1989 tells it differently. She quit in May, after a disagreement with her family over the remodelling and running of the carpet department, and he sided with them: over three years the store's other departments had grown sales by 24 per cent while carpet fell 17. Then she opened a business of her own next door, in a building she had owned for years, and at ninety-six was selling carpet and furniture against the store she had founded. At the end of 1992 she sold the building and land to the Mart and kept her carpet business running inside it. At ninety-nine she signed the non-compete Buffett had not thought to ask for when she was eighty-nine. She died on 9 August 1998, aged 104.

bio.t: Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist
bio.why: Lowenstein gives the Mart and the 1983 deal from outside the family. Alice Schroeder's 'The Snowball' (2008) has more Blumkin detail and was written with Buffett's cooperation, which is exactly why it is the second read rather than the first. For her own story in Buffett's words, the Berkshire letters for 1983, 1989, 1992 and 1993 are free to read.

contested: Why she left in 1989, and whether she was right. The only account this entry has opened is Buffett's 1989 letter, written by the man who owned most of the store she was arguing with. It credits her with more smart business decisions than any living American, notes that she personally outsold everyone on the floor, and still finds for the family on the numbers. Her side of the argument about the remodelling is not in anything opened here. The other open question is the price. Neither Berkshire letter gives one; the obituary in J. (28 August 1998) puts the deal at $55 million, and other retellings give $60 million for 90 per cent. The house prints neither as fact until a document from 1983 does.
